paraJumbles.title: The school savings club

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Last year, the club used the interest earned on this account to buy fifty storybooks for the school library.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Every Monday, the children brought whatever coins they had saved and handed them to a teacher, who recorded each deposit in a register.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: More importantly, the children have learnt that small sums, saved regularly, can grow into something truly useful.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Three years ago, a small school in a village near Nashik started a savings club for its students.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: At the end of each month, the teacher took the collected money to the nearest bank branch and deposited it in the club's account.

explanation: D opens: it introduces the savings club without referring back to anything.
B follows D: *the children* are the students of D, and B introduces *a teacher* who collects the coins.
E follows B: *the teacher* and *the collected money* both point back to B.
A follows E: *this account* is the club's bank account opened in E, and only a bank account earns interest.
C closes: *More importantly* ranks the lesson learnt above the first benefit (the books) in A.

paraJumbles.title: From queues to clicks

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: This changed when the railways launched an online booking system that allowed passengers to buy tickets from home or office.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Today, with an inexpensive smartphone in almost every pocket, most reserved tickets are booked online in a matter of minutes.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: For decades, buying a long-distance train ticket in India meant standing in a slow-moving queue at the station's reservation counter.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: At first, only people with a computer and an internet connection could use it, so the queues at stations barely shrank.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Passengers often had to take half a day off work for this, and even then a confirmed berth was not guaranteed.

explanation: C opens: it describes the old situation without referring back to anything.
E follows C: *for this* refers to standing in the queue described in C.
A follows E: *This changed* marks the turning point after the problem set out in C and E.
D follows A: *it* is the online booking system of A, and *At first* describes its early days.
B closes: *Today* completes the timeline — for decades, then the launch, at first, and today.

paraJumbles.title: Farm ponds

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: A subsidy covering most of the digging cost has changed their minds, and over four thousand ponds were dug in the region last year.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: In many dry districts of Maharashtra, farmers depend entirely on the monsoon, and a delay of even two weeks can ruin a season's crop.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Small farmers, however, were at first unwilling to give up even a corner of their land for a pond.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: To reduce this risk, many of them have begun digging farm ponds: shallow pits, lined with plastic sheets, that trap rainwater during heavy showers.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: This stored water keeps the crop alive during the dry spells that often follow, when the soil would otherwise crack and the plants wilt.

explanation: B opens: it states the problem (total dependence on the monsoon) without referring back to anything.
D follows B: *this risk* is the crop failure described in B, and *them* refers to the farmers.
E follows D: *This stored water* is the rainwater trapped by the ponds, and *the dry spells that often follow* come after the heavy showers of D.
C follows E: *however* and *at first unwilling* bring in the one drawback of the ponds after their benefit.
A closes: the subsidy *changed their minds* — the minds of the unwilling small farmers in C — and the four thousand new ponds round off the story.

paraJumbles.title: The tea stall goes digital

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: For most of that time, he accepted only cash, and on busy mornings he often ran out of change for customers carrying large notes.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: The effect was immediate: office-goers who used to walk past because they carried no cash began stopping for a cup.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Two years ago, his college-going nephew persuaded him to display a QR code so that customers could pay through UPI apps.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: His daily sales have nearly doubled since then, and he no longer keeps a tin of coins beside the stove.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Ramesh has been running a small tea stall near the bus stand in Mysuru for nearly twenty years.

explanation: E opens: it introduces Ramesh and his tea stall without referring back to anything.
A follows E: *that time* is the twenty years mentioned in E, and *he* is Ramesh.
C follows A: *Two years ago* marks the change from the cash-only years described in A.
B follows C: *The effect* is the effect of displaying the QR code, which let customers *who carried no cash* pay.
D closes: *since then* looks back to the change, and *no longer keeps a tin of coins* answers the problem of change raised in A.

paraJumbles.title: Tackling anaemia in schools

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: In districts where both steps have been followed for three years, the share of anaemic students has fallen by nearly a third.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: The good news is that the condition is easy and inexpensive to prevent, even in households with very little money.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Anaemia, a condition in which the blood carries too little oxygen, is one of the most common health problems among Indian teenagers.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Without enough haemoglobin, a teenager tires easily, struggles to concentrate in class and falls ill more often than classmates who eat well.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Many schools now hand out a weekly iron tablet, and teachers talk to students about cheap iron-rich foods such as leafy greens, jaggery and pulses.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: It usually results from a diet low in iron, the mineral the body needs to make haemoglobin.

explanation: C opens: it defines anaemia and introduces the topic without referring back to anything.
F follows C: *It* is anaemia, and F gives its cause, introducing the word *haemoglobin*.
D follows F: *Without enough haemoglobin* picks up the word just introduced in F and describes the harm.
B follows D: *The good news* turns from the harm described so far to prevention.
E gives the ways of preventing it promised in B; A closes: *both steps* are the iron tablets and the food lessons of E, and A reports the result.

paraJumbles.title: Guardians of the coast

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees that grow in the muddy strip where rivers meet the sea along India's coastline.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Mangroves also serve as nurseries for young fish and crabs, on which thousands of fishing families depend for a living.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Several coastal states are now replanting them, and satellite surveys show that the country's mangrove cover is slowly rising again.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Their dense, tangled roots trap silt and break the force of incoming waves, shielding the villages that lie behind them.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Despite these benefits, large stretches of mangrove forest were cleared in past decades to make way for salt pans, fish farms and ports.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: For this reason, coastal villages protected by thick mangrove belts have suffered far less damage in recent cyclones than exposed ones.

explanation: A opens: it defines mangroves without referring back to anything.
D follows A: *Their … roots* are the roots of the mangroves just defined.
F is fixed third and fits there: *For this reason* points back to the wave-breaking roots in D.
B follows F: *also* adds a second benefit (nurseries for fish) after the first (protection from waves).
E follows B: *Despite these benefits* sums up D, F and B before turning to the damage. C closes: *now replanting* answers the clearing described in E.

paraJumbles.title: Loans from a payment trail

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Without such documents, a lender had no reliable way to judge whether a borrower could repay, a gap that left many vendors at the mercy of moneylenders.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: The danger is that such loans will bypass the many vendors who still deal mostly in cash and so leave no digital trail.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: By studying these payment trails, some lenders now offer small loans that are repaid through tiny deductions from the vendor's daily receipts.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: For years, banks hesitated to lend to street vendors, who could show no salary slips, tax returns or any other proof of steady income.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Digital payments are quietly closing this gap, as every QR-code sale leaves a dated record of what a vendor earns each day.

explanation: D opens: it sets out the problem (no proof of income) and refers back to nothing.
A follows D: *such documents* are the salary slips and tax returns of D, and A sums the problem up as *a gap*.
E follows A: *this gap* can only point to the word *gap* in A; E cannot come earlier because no gap has been named before A.
C follows E: *these payment trails* are the daily records created by QR-code sales in E.
B closes: *such loans* are the small loans introduced in C, and *The danger is* adds the limitation that ends the paragraph.

paraJumbles.title: Self-help groups and credit

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Impressed by this record, banks began lending directly to the groups, treating their savings history as a substitute for collateral.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Yet researchers caution that credit is only a beginning, since without steady markets for their products, such businesses seldom grow.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: The pooled savings are lent to members in turn, usually for needs such as school fees, seeds or a sewing machine.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: This link with the formal banking system has allowed many members to start small businesses that they could never have financed alone.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: In many Indian villages, women have formed self-help groups of ten to twenty members who save small sums together every week.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: Because this lending rests on trust and peer pressure, repayment rates in such groups are often higher than those of ordinary commercial borrowers.

explanation: E opens: it introduces self-help groups and refers back to nothing.
C follows E: *The pooled savings* are the small sums the members save together in E.
F follows C: *this lending* is the lending of pooled savings described in C, and F reports its result — high repayment.
A follows F: *this record* is the repayment record of F, which is why the banks started lending.
D follows A: *This link with the formal banking system* is the bank lending of A. B closes: *Yet* adds a caution, and *such businesses* are the ones started in D.

paraJumbles.title: The revival of block printing

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Over the last two decades, however, designers and online stores have built a new market among buyers willing to pay more for handmade cloth.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: This means the printer must press the same stretch of cloth up to a dozen times, letting each colour dry in between.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Hand block printing, in which carved wooden blocks are dipped in dye and pressed onto cloth, has been practised in parts of Rajasthan for centuries.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: As a result, younger members of these families are returning to the workshops, often pairing the old blocks with designs of their own.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Such slow, painstaking work could not compete when cheap screen-printed fabrics flooded the market, and many printing families abandoned the craft.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: Every block is carved by hand, and a single design may need a dozen of them, one for each colour it contains.

explanation: C opens: it defines hand block printing and refers back to nothing.
F follows C: *Every block* refers to the carved blocks of C, and F adds that one design needs a dozen of them.
B follows F: *This means* draws the consequence of needing a dozen blocks — up to a dozen pressings of the same cloth.
E, fixed fourth, follows B: *Such slow, painstaking work* sums up the process in B.
A follows E: *however* turns from the decline to the revival. D closes: *As a result* follows from the new market in A, and *these families* are the printing families of E.

paraJumbles.title: Cold rooms at the farm gate

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Investors have been slow to build such a network because farmers rarely rent storage, and farmers rarely rent it because none exists nearby.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Their running costs, however, are negligible, and since space is rented by the crate, even a farmer with half an acre of tomatoes can use them.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Early trials suggest that farmers who hold back their produce for a week or two, instead of selling at harvest-time prices, earn about a quarter more.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Every year, a large share of India's fruit and vegetables rots before reaching a consumer, even as city shoppers complain of high prices.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Small solar-powered cold rooms, though costly to install, offer a way out of this impasse because they can be placed at the edge of a village.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: The culprit is not a shortage of produce but the lack of a cold chain, the network of refrigerated stores and vehicles that keeps harvests fresh.

explanation: D opens: it states the paradox (food rots while prices stay high) and refers back to nothing.
F follows D: *The culprit* names the cause of the waste in D and introduces the cold chain as a *network*.
A follows F: *such a network* can only be the cold chain of F; A describes a circular stand-off between investors and farmers.
E follows A: *this impasse* is the stand-off in A, and E admits that the cold rooms are *costly to install*.

B follows E: *Their running costs, however* contrasts with *costly to install*, and *Their* must refer to the cold rooms. C closes: farmers can *hold back their produce* only once the storage of E and B exists, and C gives the result.

paraJumbles.title: Bags from old saris

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Within a year, the group was supplying more than two hundred shops, and each member was earning a steady monthly income.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: When the town of Kolhapur banned thin plastic carry bags, shopkeepers and customers alike wondered how they would manage.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Their success shows that a rule meant to protect the environment can also create work for those who respond to it quickly.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: A women's self-help group in one ward saw an opportunity in this confusion and began stitching cloth bags from old saris and leftover fabric.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: They offered these bags to vegetable vendors and grocers at a few rupees each, and the first shopkeepers who tried them soon asked for more.

explanation: B opens: it describes the plastic-bag ban without referring back to anything.
D follows B: *this confusion* is the worry of shopkeepers and customers in B.
E follows D: *They* are the women of the group and *these bags* are the cloth bags they began stitching in D.
A follows E: the shopkeepers who *asked for more* in E lead to the group supplying over two hundred shops *within a year*.
C closes: *Their success* sums up the growth in A and draws the lesson.

paraJumbles.title: Village seed banks

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Over the years, many of them gave up this practice and began buying hybrid seeds, which promised higher yields.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: A farmer who borrows seed from the bank returns twice the amount after the harvest, so that the stock keeps growing year after year.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: With fewer farmers growing them, many of these old varieties, suited to local soils and rainfall, have almost disappeared.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: These seeds, however, have to be bought afresh every season, and they often need more water and fertiliser than the old local varieties.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: In the past, farmers in most Indian villages kept aside a portion of each harvest as seed for the next season.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: To save what remains, some villages have set up community seed banks, where farmers deposit a small quantity of local seed after the harvest.

explanation: E opens: it describes the old practice of saving seed and refers back to nothing.
A follows E: *many of them* are the farmers of E and *this practice* is saving seed.
D follows A: *These seeds* are the hybrid seeds of A, and *however* introduces their drawbacks, ending with *the old local varieties*.
C follows D: *these old varieties* can only point to *the old local varieties* named at the end of D.
F follows C: *what remains* is what is left of the disappearing varieties in C. B closes: *the bank* is the community seed bank set up in F.

paraJumbles.title: Tolls without stopping

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: The tag is linked to the owner's bank account or wallet, and a reader at the plaza deducts the toll as the vehicle passes.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: The next step being tested is a system that charges vehicles by the exact distance they travel, so that toll plazas may one day disappear altogether.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: At busy plazas, the queues could stretch for over a kilometre, wasting fuel and adding hours to a journey.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Because vehicles no longer have to stop, waiting times at plazas have fallen sharply, although unread tags and wrong charges still lead to complaints.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: To end these delays, the government made it compulsory for vehicles to carry an electronic tag stuck to the windscreen.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: Until a few years ago, a long drive on an Indian highway meant stopping at every toll plaza to pay in cash.

explanation: F opens: it describes the old system and refers back to nothing.
C follows F: *the queues* at *busy plazas* are the result of every vehicle stopping to pay in cash.
E is fixed third and fits there: *these delays* are the long queues and lost hours of C.
A follows E: *The tag* is the electronic tag introduced in E, and A explains how the toll is deducted *as the vehicle passes*.
D follows A: *no longer have to stop* depends on the toll being deducted as the vehicle passes. B closes: *The next step* goes beyond the tag system to a future without plazas.

paraJumbles.title: Buy now, pay later

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Such penalties can mount quickly, and because the schemes are easy to join, some users end up juggling several at once without a clear idea of what they owe.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: It is this apparent absence of cost that has made them popular among young consumers, many of whom have never held a credit card.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Regulators have therefore begun to insist that these lenders check a borrower's ability to repay and report the loans to credit bureaus, just as banks do.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Unlike a credit card, which earns its issuer interest on unpaid balances, these schemes make money chiefly from fees charged to merchants and penalties on customers who miss a payment.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Buy-now-pay-later schemes let shoppers split the price of a purchase into small instalments, often without paying any interest if they pay on time.

explanation: E opens: it defines buy-now-pay-later schemes and refers back to nothing.
B follows E: *this apparent absence of cost* can only be the interest-free instalments of E, and *them* are the schemes.
D follows B: *Unlike a credit card* picks up the credit card mentioned at the end of B and explains how the schemes really earn money.
A follows D: *Such penalties* are the penalties on customers who miss a payment in D; no other sentence mentions penalties.
C closes: *therefore* draws the regulatory response from the mounting debts in A, and *these lenders* are the scheme providers.

paraJumbles.title: Smaller packets, same price

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Yet the tactic is not without peril, for consumers who eventually discover that they are paying the same for less often feel they have been deceived.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Increasingly, firms have found a way to sidestep this dilemma, leaving the price untouched while quietly trimming the quantity in each packet.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Such resentment can do more lasting damage to a brand than an honest price rise would have done, which is why some firms now announce the change openly.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Either course is unattractive: the first risks driving customers to cheaper rivals, while the second eats into profits.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Economists call this 'shrinkflation', and it works because shoppers notice a change in price far more readily than a change in weight.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: When the cost of raw materials rises, a maker of packaged food must decide whether to pass the increase on to shoppers or to absorb it.

explanation: F opens: it sets out the manufacturer's choice and refers back to nothing.
D follows F: *Either course*, *the first* and *the second* need the two options — passing on or absorbing the increase — named in F.
B follows D: *this dilemma* is the choice between two unattractive courses described in F and D.
E follows B: *this* in *Economists call this 'shrinkflation'* is the practice of trimming the quantity described in B.
A follows E: *Yet* turns from why the tactic works (E) to its danger. C closes: *Such resentment* is the feeling of being deceived in A.

paraJumbles.title: The lake that came back

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: With only clean rainwater flowing in, the lake filled up during the next monsoon, and migratory birds returned to it for the first time in years.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Until a few years ago, Kalyani Lake, on the edge of a small town near Mysuru, was little more than a muddy pond choked with weeds and plastic.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Today, the residents who once spent their Sundays hauling out plastic spend them counting the birds instead.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Their efforts caught the attention of the town council, which then blocked the drains that had been carrying sewage into the lake.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Worried that it would soon disappear altogether, a group of residents began meeting at its edge every Sunday morning to pull out the rubbish by hand.

explanation: B opens: it introduces the lake and its sorry state without referring back to anything.
E follows B: *it* is the lake, and the fear that it *would soon disappear* comes from the shrinking pond described in B.
D follows E: *Their efforts* are the Sunday clean-ups by the residents in E.
A follows D: *only clean rainwater flowing in* is possible because the council blocked the sewage drains in D.
C closes: *Today* ends the time chain, and *hauling out plastic* and *counting the birds* look back to E and A.

paraJumbles.title: From cane juice to jaggery

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: When the liquid has thickened into a golden paste, it is moved to a shallow trough and stirred constantly as it cools.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: This juice is then poured into a wide iron pan and boiled for several hours, while workers skim off the scum that rises to the top.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Finally, the half-set mass is pressed into moulds or shaped by hand into blocks, ready to be packed and sold.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Jaggery, the unrefined sugar used in many Indian sweets, is still made in small village units in much the same way as it was a century ago.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: First, freshly cut sugarcane is crushed between heavy rollers to squeeze out its juice.

explanation: D opens: it introduces jaggery and its traditional making without referring back to anything.
E follows D: *First* begins the process, and the cane is crushed to give juice.
B follows E: *This juice* is the juice squeezed out in E, and *then* marks the next step.
A follows B: *the liquid* is the boiling juice of B, which has now *thickened*.
C closes: *Finally* marks the last step, and *the half-set mass* is the cooling paste of A.

paraJumbles.title: Teenagers short of sleep

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: To give the hormone a chance to work, the researchers have urged parents to keep phones out of bedrooms at night, a rule that costs nothing and could restore much of the lost sleep.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: The main culprit, according to the same survey, is the mobile phone: nearly two-thirds of the students admitted to using one in bed after the lights were off.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: The light from such screens delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that tells the body it is time to sleep, so even a few minutes of scrolling can keep a teenager awake for an hour.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: This falls well short of the eight to ten hours that doctors recommend for this age group, since the body and brain do much of their growing and repair during sleep.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: A recent survey of over five thousand schoolchildren in six Indian cities found that more than half of those aged fourteen to seventeen sleep less than seven hours a night.

explanation: E opens: *A recent survey* introduces the topic and the key figure (less than seven hours) without referring back to anything.
D follows E: *This falls well short* compares the survey figure in E with the recommended hours; no other sentence gives a number of hours for D to refer to.
B follows D: *The main culprit* names the cause of the shortfall, and *the same survey* points back to E.
C follows B: *such screens* are the mobile phones of B, and C explains how they keep teenagers awake.
A closes: *the hormone* can only be the melatonin named in C, so A cannot come before C; *the lost sleep* rounds off the problem set out in E.

paraJumbles.title: Grandmother's pickles

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Word spread quickly, and within a year orders were arriving from as far away as Delhi and Kolkata, far more than her kitchen could handle.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: To keep up, she rented a small unit, hired six women from her locality and, after much hesitation, listed her pickles on a large online marketplace.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: When Leela Thomas lost her office job in Kochi, she began selling the mango and lime pickles that her grandmother had taught her to make.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: That decision transformed the business: her brand now sells in four countries, yet every batch is still made from her grandmother's recipes.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: At first, her only customers were neighbours and former colleagues, who placed their orders through a messaging group she had set up.

explanation: C opens: it introduces Leela Thomas and how the pickle business began, without referring back to anything.
E follows C: *At first* describes the earliest customers of the business started in C.
A follows E: *Word spread* from those first customers, and the orders grew to be *far more than her kitchen could handle*.
B follows A: *To keep up* answers the flood of orders in A; B cannot come earlier because nothing before A needs keeping up with.
D closes: *That decision* is the move to the online marketplace at the end of B, and D reports the result.

paraJumbles.title: The first train

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: On 16 April 1853, India's first passenger train left Bori Bunder in Bombay for Thane, a journey of about 34 kilometres.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: This network was built mainly to carry raw cotton and other goods to the ports, but ordinary Indians soon took to it in numbers that surprised its builders.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Their wonder did not last long, for within three decades the railways had grown into a network of several thousand miles of track.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: By the end of the century, the crowded third-class carriage had become one of the few places where people of every background travelled side by side.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Thousands of curious onlookers lined the route that afternoon, many of them convinced that the smoking engine was some kind of living beast.

explanation: A opens: it gives the date and the event, the first passenger train, and refers back to nothing.
E follows A: *that afternoon* is the day of the first run, and *the smoking engine* is the engine of that train.
C follows E: *Their wonder* is the amazement of the onlookers in E, and *within three decades* moves the time chain forward.
B follows C: *This network* can only be the network of track named at the end of C.
D closes: *By the end of the century* is the last step in the time chain, and the crowded third-class carriage shows the ordinary passengers of B.

paraJumbles.title: Blurred blackboards

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Most of them are short-sighted: their eyeballs have grown slightly too long, so that distant objects look blurred.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Eye doctors in Indian cities are reporting a sharp rise in the number of schoolchildren who need spectacles to read the blackboard clearly.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Daylight, on the other hand, appears to slow it down, which is why children who play outdoors for a couple of hours a day are much less likely to need glasses.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Such growth, studies suggest, is encouraged by long hours of close-up work, such as reading from a phone held a few inches from the face.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Doctors therefore advise parents to limit screen time and send children out to play every day, advice that costs nothing and may save a child's eyesight.

explanation: B opens: it reports the rise in children needing spectacles and refers back to nothing.
A follows B: *them* are the schoolchildren of B, and A explains what is wrong with their eyes.
D follows A: *Such growth* is the lengthening of the eyeball described in A.
C follows D: *on the other hand* sets daylight against the close-up work of D, and *it* is the same growth, which daylight slows.
E closes: *therefore* turns the two findings of D and C (less screen time, more outdoor play) into advice.

paraJumbles.title: Certificates on the phone

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Government-backed digital lockers now offer a way around this paperwork, letting citizens keep official copies of their certificates on their phones.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Some offices, however, still insist on paper, so the old file of photocopies has not yet disappeared entirely.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Collecting these attestations could take days, and a single lost mark sheet might mean months of letters to a distant board.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Because the copies in these lockers are issued directly by the boards and departments concerned, an institution that receives one can be sure that it has not been tampered with.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Applying for a scholarship, a job or a bank loan in India once meant carrying a thick file of photocopied certificates, each attested by a gazetted officer.

explanation: E opens: it describes the old practice of carrying attested photocopies and refers back to nothing.
C follows E: *these attestations* are the officer's attestations on the photocopies of E.
A follows C: *this paperwork* sums up the attesting and the letters of E and C, and *now* brings in the new solution.
D follows A: *these lockers* are the digital lockers introduced in A, and D gives their main advantage.
B closes: *however* adds the limitation, and *the old file of photocopies* looks back to the opening sentence.

paraJumbles.title: Why cities flood

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: In a city paved with concrete and asphalt, very little of it can soak into the soil, so almost all of it rushes into drains built for far smaller towns.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Such spaces cost far less than rebuilding an entire drainage network, and they also help to refill the groundwater that cities pump out every summer.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Some city planners are now trying to reverse this by creating 'sponge' areas, such as parks, lakes and rain gardens that hold rainwater and let it sink slowly into the earth.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Every monsoon, streets in several Indian cities turn into rivers after just a few hours of heavy rain.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: The rain itself is rarely the real problem; the trouble lies in where the water goes once it reaches the ground.

explanation: D opens: it states the problem (flooded streets) and refers back to nothing.
E follows D: *The rain itself* picks up the heavy rain of D and shifts the blame to where the water goes.
A follows E: it answers the question raised in E, and *it* is the water that reaches the ground.
C follows A: *reverse this* means letting water soak into the ground instead of rushing into drains, the cause given in A.
B closes: *Such spaces* are the parks, lakes and rain gardens of C, and B adds their further benefits.

paraJumbles.title: Bees on guard

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: In villages on the edge of forests in southern India, herds of wild elephants often raid fields at night, destroying a season's crop in a few hours.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: A gentler answer has come from an unexpected source: the honeybee, which elephants go out of their way to avoid.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: The hives pay for themselves, too, as the farmers sell the honey they produce.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Farmers have tried everything from firecrackers to electric fences to drive them away, but the first soon stop scaring the animals and the second can kill them.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: In trials, strings of beehives hung on a wire around a field kept most herds out, because an elephant that brushed against the wire set off a buzzing swarm.

explanation: A opens: it describes the elephant raids and refers back to nothing.
D follows A: *them* are the elephants of A, and *the first … the second* need the two methods named in D itself.
B follows D: *A gentler answer* is set against the cruel and useless methods of D.
E follows B: it shows how the honeybee of B is put to work, introducing *beehives* hung on a wire.
C closes: *The hives* can only be the beehives of E, and *too* adds a second benefit to the protection of the crop.

paraJumbles.title: Groceries in ten minutes

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: This model, however, is costly to run, and most of the companies behind it are still losing money on every order.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: The speed comes not from faster riders but from a network of 'dark stores', small warehouses that are closed to shoppers and placed within two or three kilometres of the customers they serve.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Ten-minute grocery delivery, unheard of in India until a few years ago, is now routine in most large cities.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Their bet is that customers, once used to such convenience, will keep coming back even after delivery fees are raised.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Each of these stores stocks only the few thousand items that sell most often in its neighbourhood, so a worker can pack an order in under two minutes.

explanation: C opens: it introduces ten-minute delivery and refers back to nothing.
B follows C: *The speed* is the ten-minute delivery of C, and B introduces the dark stores.
E follows B: *these stores* are the dark stores of B.
A follows E: *This model* is the dark-store system described in B and E, and *however* turns to its cost.
D closes: *Their bet* is the bet of *the companies* in A, which keep losing money in the hope of raising fees later.

paraJumbles.title: A bank in the front room

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Until 2018, the nearest bank branch to Bhimpur, a village in Odisha, was eighteen kilometres away, and a round trip cost a full day's wages.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Her success has since persuaded the bank to appoint correspondents in eleven neighbouring villages.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Within months, elderly villagers who had once lost a day's wages to collect a pension of a few hundred rupees could receive it a few steps from home.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: That year, Sunita, a graduate from the village, was appointed its business correspondent, an agent who offers basic banking services on behalf of a bank.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Armed with a fingerprint scanner and a small printer, she began opening accounts, accepting deposits and paying out pensions from a desk in her own front room.

explanation: A opens: it sets the scene (no bank nearby) and refers back to nothing.
D follows A: *That year* is 2018, the year named in A, and *its* refers to the village.
E follows D: *she* is Sunita, and E describes the work of the correspondent introduced in D.
C follows E: *a few steps from home* is the desk in her front room, and *once lost a day's wages* recalls the costly trip of A.
B closes: *Her success* sums up E and C, and *since* looks back from the present.

paraJumbles.title: Compost in two pots

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: The first pot is lined with a layer of dry leaves, and the day's kitchen scraps are added on top, each new layer being covered with a handful of dry material.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: By the time the second pot fills up, the contents of the first will have turned into a dark, crumbly compost that smells of damp earth.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Nearly half of the rubbish thrown out by an average Indian household is wet kitchen waste, such as vegetable peels, tea leaves and leftover food.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: This compost can be mixed into the soil of potted plants or a kitchen garden, carrying the waste from the kitchen back to the plate.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Once this pot is full, it is covered and left to rest, while the family begins filling the second one in the same way.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: Instead of sending it to a landfill, where it rots and gives off methane, a family can turn it into compost within a few weeks using nothing more than two earthen pots.

explanation: C opens: it introduces wet kitchen waste and refers back to nothing.
F follows C: *it* is the wet waste of C, and F introduces the *two earthen pots*.
A follows F: *The first pot* is the first of the two pots named in F.
E follows A: *this pot* is the first pot being filled in A, and E starts on *the second one*.
B follows E: *By the time the second pot fills up* needs the filling of the second pot begun in E. D closes: *This compost* is the dark, crumbly compost of B.

paraJumbles.title: Partners without protection

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Yet the same freedom becomes a burden when a rider is hurt in a road accident, since a day off the road is a day without pay and there is no employer to meet the hospital bill.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: A government think-tank study estimated that India had nearly eight million gig workers at the start of this decade, a number it expected to triple by 2030.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: The arrangement suits many workers, who value being able to log in and out whenever they please.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: A few states have responded by setting up welfare boards funded by a small levy on each order, an approach that keeps the flexibility while offering a basic safety net.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Most of them are classified not as employees but as 'partners', a label that frees the platforms from paying for pensions, health insurance or paid leave.

explanation: B opens: *A government think-tank study* introduces gig workers and their number without referring back to anything.
E follows B: *them* are the gig workers of B, and E explains the 'partner' label.
C follows E: *The arrangement* is being classed as a partner rather than an employee; C cannot follow B directly because B describes no arrangement.
A follows C: *the same freedom* is the freedom to log in and out in C, so A must come immediately after it; *Yet* turns the advantage into a burden.
D closes: *responded* answers the problem in A, and *keeps the flexibility while offering a basic safety net* balances the advantage of C against the risk of A.

paraJumbles.title: Antibiotics losing ground

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: To deny the bacteria these easy chances, regulators have begun inspecting pharmacies and fining those that sell antibiotics without a prescription.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: In India, this process has been speeded up by the easy sale of antibiotics over the counter, often for colds and fevers caused by viruses.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: The reason lies in evolution: whenever a dose is taken, the few bacteria that happen to survive it multiply and pass on their resistance.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Since antibiotics have no effect on viruses, each such dose brings the patient no benefit while handing the bacteria in the body one more chance to adapt.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Antibiotics, which turned many once-deadly infections into minor illnesses during the last century, are steadily losing their power.

explanation: E opens: it states the problem (antibiotics losing their power) and refers back to nothing.
C follows E: *The reason* explains why antibiotics are losing their power, and C describes how resistance spreads.
B follows C: *this process* is the spread of resistance described in C, and B introduces over-the-counter sales for viral illnesses.
D follows B: *viruses* and *each such dose* point to the antibiotics bought for viral colds and fevers in B; D also introduces the *chance to adapt* that A picks up.
A closes: *these easy chances* are the chances to adapt handed to the bacteria in D, and the regulators' crackdown on sales without a prescription ends the paragraph.

paraJumbles.title: A familiar voice

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: The trick used to fail more often than not, because a parent could usually tell that the voice on the line was not really their son's.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: The recordings it needs are easy to find, since many people post videos of themselves on social media without a second thought.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Fraudsters have long posed as relatives in trouble, phoning elderly people to ask for urgent money for a hospital bill or a police fine.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Cheap software that can copy a voice from a few seconds of recorded speech has now removed that safeguard.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Since almost anyone's voice is thus within a fraudster's reach, police advise families to agree on a secret word that any member asking for money in an emergency must be able to say.

explanation: C opens: it describes an old kind of fraud and refers back to nothing.
A follows C: *The trick* is the fraudsters' pretence in C, and A explains why it often failed.
D follows A: *that safeguard* is the parent's ability to recognise the voice, described in A.
B follows D: *it* is the voice-copying software of D, and *The recordings it needs* are the *few seconds of recorded speech*.
E closes: *thus within a fraudster's reach* sums up D and B (cheap copying software and easily found recordings), and the secret word is the answer to a voice that can no longer be trusted.

paraJumbles.title: The wheat revolution

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Punjab, with its canals and enterprising farmers, took to the new seeds fastest, and within a few years its wheat harvest had nearly doubled.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Determined to end this dependence, the government promoted new dwarf varieties of wheat that yielded far more grain per acre, provided they were given plenty of water and fertiliser.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Agricultural experts now argue that the region must shift part of its land to crops that need less water, even if these earn its farmers less.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: In the mid-1960s, two successive droughts left India so short of grain that it had to depend on large shipments of imported wheat to feed its people.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: The very conditions that made this leap possible have since become a source of worry, however, for decades of heavy pumping to water the thirsty crops have drained the state's underground reserves.

explanation: D opens: *In the mid-1960s* sets the starting point of the time chain, and D refers back to nothing.
B follows D: *this dependence* is the reliance on imported wheat in D, and B brings in the new varieties.
A follows B: *the new seeds* are the dwarf varieties of B.
E follows A: *this leap* is the near-doubling of the harvest in A, and *The very conditions* are the water and fertiliser the seeds needed (stated in B).
C closes: *the region* is Punjab, and the experts' advice to grow less thirsty crops answers the falling water reserves of E.

paraJumbles.title: Smoke from the fields

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Many experts therefore favour village hiring centres, where a farmer can rent such a machine for a few days instead of buying one outright.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: There, farmers set fire to the stubble left behind after the rice harvest, because the window before wheat must be sown is barely three weeks long.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Machines that sow wheat straight through the stubble offer a way out, but they are expensive and stand idle for most of the year.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Clearing the straw by hand or by machine in that time costs money that most of them do not have, whereas a matchstick costs almost nothing.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Every November, a thick haze settles over Delhi, and part of it drifts in from fields hundreds of kilometres away in Punjab and Haryana.

explanation: E opens: it describes the haze over Delhi and refers back to nothing.
B follows E: *There* can only mean the fields in Punjab and Haryana named in E.
D follows B: *that time* is the three-week window of B, and *them* are the farmers.
C follows D: *a way out* answers the farmers' bind in D, but *expensive* and *idle for most of the year* raise a new difficulty.
A closes: *therefore* and *such a machine* point to the costly, rarely used machines of C, which renting solves; A cannot come before C because no machine has been named.

paraJumbles.title: The middle-sized tub

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Few people actually buy the medium tub, but that is not why it is on the menu.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Once you know the trick, you begin to see it everywhere, from mobile data plans to magazine subscriptions.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Its real purpose is to make the large tub look like a bargain, since for just a few rupees more the customer gets almost twice as much.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Cinema halls often sell popcorn in three sizes, and the medium one is usually priced only a little below the large.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Economists call an option that exists only to steer buyers in this way a 'decoy', and experiments show that adding one can shift many buyers towards the costliest choice.

explanation: D opens: it describes the three sizes of popcorn and refers back to nothing.
A follows D: *the medium tub* is the medium size of D, and *that is not why it is on the menu* raises a question.
C follows A: *Its real purpose* answers the question raised in A; *real* is set against the reason that A rejects.
E follows C: *steer buyers in this way* needs the steering towards the large tub described in C, so E cannot come straight after A.
B closes: *the trick* is the decoy named in E, and B widens it to other products.

paraJumbles.title: What a deposit really earns

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: And since the interest itself is taxed, a depositor in a higher tax bracket may find that even this thin margin disappears.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: If a deposit earns seven per cent a year while prices rise by six, the saver is only one per cent better off in terms of what the money can buy.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Many Indian households still keep their savings in fixed deposits, trusting that the money is both safe and growing.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Safe it may be, but whether it is growing depends on something few depositors check: the rate at which prices are rising.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: This is why financial planners urge savers to judge an investment by its real return, the interest earned minus inflation and tax, rather than by the rate printed on the receipt.

explanation: C opens: it introduces fixed deposits and the belief that the money is *safe and growing*, without referring back to anything.
D follows C: *Safe it may be* takes up the word *safe* in C and questions the word *growing*.
B follows D: it works out an example of the price rise mentioned in D, ending with a gain of *one per cent*.
A follows B: *this thin margin* is the one per cent of B, and *And since* adds tax as a second drain.
E closes: *This is why* draws the lesson from B and A, and *minus inflation and tax* sums up both.

paraJumbles.title: Millets back on the plate

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: For centuries, millets such as ragi, jowar and bajra were the staple grains of farming families across the drier parts of India.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Today the company sells in over two thousand stores, and its success has persuaded far larger food firms to launch millet ranges of their own.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: That expectation proved easy to overturn once the brand began handing out free samples at gyms and offices, where buyers found that the products tasted much like the ones they already ate.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: A decade ago, two friends from Pune set out to change this image, launching a brand that sold millets as breakfast flakes, noodles and biscuits.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: From the 1970s onwards, cheap rice and wheat sold through ration shops pushed them off most plates, and they came to be seen as the food of the poor.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: Sales in the first year were dismal, as city shoppers had no idea how to cook the grain and expected it to taste coarse.

explanation: A opens: *For centuries* begins the time chain and introduces millets without referring back to anything.
E follows A: *them* and *they* are the millets of A, and *From the 1970s onwards* moves the story forward.
D follows E: *this image* is the idea in E that millets are the food of the poor.
F follows D: *Sales in the first year* are the first sales of the brand launched in D.
C follows F: *That expectation* is the shoppers' expectation in F that the grain would taste coarse. B closes: *Today* ends the time chain with the brand's success.

paraJumbles.title: Counting losses from space

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Insurers are now turning to satellites, which can photograph every field in a district within days and reveal from the colour of the vegetation how badly each one has suffered.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Such sample harvests are slow, and because millions of them are needed each season, many are done carelessly or not at all.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Radar sensors, which can see through cloud, are therefore being added to the system, and early trials suggest that they can cut the time taken to settle a claim by more than half.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: These images are far from perfect, though, since clouds can hide the ground during exactly the stormy weeks when damage is most likely.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: When hail or floods damage a crop, an insured farmer in India has traditionally had to wait for officials to harvest and weigh a sample patch of the field to estimate the loss.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: As a result, claims are often settled months after the damage, by which time the farmer may have borrowed from a moneylender to sow the next crop.

explanation: E opens: it describes the traditional way of assessing crop loss and refers back to nothing.
B follows E: *Such sample harvests* are the sample patches harvested and weighed in E.
F follows B: *As a result* gives the consequence of the slow, careless harvests in B: late settlement of claims.
A follows F: *now turning to satellites* brings in the remedy only after the problem (slow sample harvests and late claims) has been set out in E, B and F.
D follows A: *These images* are the satellite photographs of A, and *though* adds their weakness. C closes: radar *which can see through cloud* is *therefore* added to fix the cloud problem of D.

paraJumbles.title: More efficient, more consumed

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: The coal saved by each engine, in other words, was swamped by the coal burnt in all these new ones.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons pointed to a puzzle that troubled his contemporaries: as steam engines grew more efficient, Britain was burning more coal, not less.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: None of this means that efficiency is futile; it means only that, without some check on use, efficiency alone cannot be relied upon to cut total consumption.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Economists have since found the same pattern far from the coalfields, in fuel-efficient cars that end up being driven further and in LED bulbs left burning all night because they cost so little to run.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Cheaper power, it turned out, had made engines worth installing in thousands of workshops and mills that could never before have afforded to run them.

explanation: B opens: *In 1865* and the introduction of Jevons and his puzzle set the scene; B refers back to nothing.
E follows B: *it turned out* signals the solution to the puzzle posed in B.

A follows E: *in other words* restates E as a sum, and *all these new ones* are the engines newly installed in the workshops and mills of E; after B alone, *these new ones* would have nothing to refer to.
D follows A: *the same pattern* is the saving per unit being swamped by greater use, and *since* moves from Jevons's time to the present.
C closes: *None of this* sums up all the examples in B–D and draws the balanced conclusion.

paraJumbles.title: Counting only the winners

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Business magazines are fond of profiling founders who dropped out of college and went on to build hugely successful companies.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: This silence of the failures produces a distortion that statisticians call 'survivorship bias', the habit of judging a strategy only by the cases that came through a test while ignoring those that fell by the way.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Read enough of these profiles, and it becomes tempting to conclude that leaving one's studies early is a sound strategy for anyone with a bold idea.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Guarding against it means asking, of any impressive set of examples, not merely how many succeeded but how many tried.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Such a conclusion, however, overlooks the far larger number of dropouts whose ventures failed, none of whom is ever profiled, because failure seldom makes the news.

explanation: A opens: it introduces the magazine profiles of college dropouts and refers back to nothing.
C follows A: *these profiles* are the magazine profiles of A, and C states the tempting conclusion.
E follows C: *Such a conclusion* is the conclusion drawn in C, and *however* exposes its flaw — the unprofiled failures.
B follows E: *This silence of the failures* needs the failures that are *never profiled* and never *make the news* in E; it cannot follow C, where no failure has yet been mentioned.
D closes: *it* is the survivorship bias named in B, and D gives the remedy.

paraJumbles.title: The hidden cost of a guarantee

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: In India, as in most countries, this limit is set high enough to protect the vast majority of depositors in full, leaving only the largest balances partly exposed.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Bank runs have a self-fulfilling quality: if enough depositors fear that a bank will fail and rush to withdraw their money, the bank may fail for that very reason.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Freed from that scrutiny, a poorly run bank can attract deposits simply by offering a slightly higher rate of interest, and then take risks it would otherwise have avoided.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Deposit insurance was devised to break this spiral by assuring savers that their money, up to a limit, is safe even if the bank collapses.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Economists call this 'moral hazard', and it is precisely why the limit exists: the holders of those largest balances, who still stand to lose, are left with a reason to keep watch.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: Such near-complete protection carries a hidden cost, however, for depositors who no longer fear losing their money have little reason to check how carefully a bank lends it.

explanation: B opens: it explains how bank runs feed on themselves and refers back to nothing.
D follows B: *this spiral* is the self-fulfilling run of B, and D introduces deposit insurance *up to a limit*.
A follows D: *this limit* is the limit mentioned in D, and A adds that it protects most depositors *in full*, leaving only the largest balances exposed.
F follows A: *Such near-complete protection* echoes *protect the vast majority of depositors in full* in A; D alone, which stresses a limit, does not support *near-complete*.
C follows F: *that scrutiny* is the checking of a bank's lending mentioned in F. E closes: *this* is the risk-taking of C, and *those largest balances* can only be the ones left exposed in A.

paraJumbles.title: The cobra effect

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Modern examples are not hard to find, from call centres that judge staff by how short their calls are, only to find customers cut off mid-sentence, to schools ranked on pass rates that quietly discourage weak students from sitting the exam.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: When the officials discovered the trick and scrapped the reward, the breeders, now left with worthless snakes, simply let them loose.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: For a while the scheme seemed to work, as thousands of carcasses were handed in and the payments mounted.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: The city thus ended up with more cobras than it had at the start, which is why economists now speak of a 'cobra effect' whenever an incentive worsens the very problem it was meant to solve.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Before long, however, enterprising residents realised that it was easier to breed cobras than to hunt them, and the farms they set up kept the rewards flowing.

sentences.label: F
sentences.text: According to a well-known story from colonial Delhi, officials alarmed by the number of venomous snakes in the city offered a cash reward for every dead cobra brought to them.

explanation: F opens: it introduces the story and the reward scheme without referring back to anything.
C follows F: *the scheme* is the cash reward of F, and *For a while* marks its early success.
E follows C: *Before long, however* turns from the early success to the residents' trick of breeding cobras.
B follows E: *the trick* is the breeding of E, and *the breeders* are the residents who set up the farms.
D follows B: *thus* draws the result of the released snakes in B — more cobras than before — and names the 'cobra effect'. A closes: *Modern examples* are fresh cases of the effect defined in D.
